title: Tobin's Blue Surprise
markdown:
The Azure Canal print workshop did not smell of ordinary ink. The black was a twilight black, the colour just before stars decide to show themselves, and it whispered if you were the sort of otter who listened. The air buzzed with oranges, zesty enough to make whiskers go wild. Tobin the otter, chief archivist, took his job more seriously than a badger takes a burrow. Today the tide was a deadline, and deadlines were usually more troublesome than water.

Historical pamphlets. Not souvenir fluff. They needed a print so precise, so reverent, it was almost holy. Tobin had charts. He had checklists. His sense of order could have rivalled the neatest line of canal boats on a calm morning.

“Page one, clean,” he muttered, nudging crisp parchment. “Page two, perfect. No fancy doodads unless it’s drainpipe maintenance. Who asks for flair on drainpipes? Honestly.”

He began the delicate dance of the press. A lever here. A roller there. The machine smelled of oil and citrus and old cotton rags. Each move was smooth, practised, the sort of motion you could set a clock by if clocks were otters. The first pages came out crisp, letters sharp as a new chisel, margins obedient as canal banks. Tobin allowed himself a tiny whiskery smile. This was his kingdom. The pamphlets would go out into the world looking as if history had never spilled.

Then it was not a bang. It was a tiny hum, a whisper of vibration that tickled his paws through the floorboards and up into the press’s belly. The next batch emerged still warm. Tobin blinked behind his spectacles. The ink was not its usual serious black. It was a surprising shimmering blue, like the deepest canal at dawn, and it had decided to travel. Swirling patterns, wholly unintentional, danced across the text like mischievous sprites taking the towpath without a ticket.

“Oh, dear.” His whiskers drooped. “This won’t do at all.” He set the misprinted pages aside with a sigh that sounded like a thousand overdue invoices.

Bartholomew, a junior apprentice with ink-stained fingers and eyes that missed nothing, peered over his shoulder. “Master Tobin,” he said, hushed with wonder, “these are magnificent.”

Tobin stared. “Magnificent? Bartholomew, they’re a mess.”

“The colour! The patterns — they look like the canal after a storm, when the water plays. As if the canal itself is telling a story.”

Before Tobin could answer with logic and checklists, the workshop door creaked. Rhea the kestrel, his most trusted friend, landed on a high beam. Her keen eyes scanned the scene.

“Tobin,” she called, bright, “what’s this magnificent mess?”

“A disaster, Rhea.” He tried to smooth his ruffled dignity. “I asked for subtle. I got a banner. A very pretty, very incorrect banner.”

Rhea ruffled her feathers. “Incorrect, perhaps. Look around. Everyone’s gathered. They’re not complaining. They’re admiring.”

And they were. Other apprentices had clustered. Even Lord Ashworth himself, a portly gentleman with a magnificent beard, stood among them. The usual clatter had become hushed admiration. The blue shimmered. The patterns drew the eye like forgotten stars. Tobin’s reputation prickled. He tried to explain, to fix it. The press, as if sensing his distress, sputtered and coughed and produced an even more vibrant chaos of blue swirls.

“It’s the press!” he wailed. “It’s gone rogue! It’s developing a mind of its own!”

Rhea swooped down, a gentle flutter beside him. “Perhaps,” she said, gaze steady. “Or perhaps you’ve made something unexpected. Something that looks like a mistake and feels right. That canal magic Bartholomew mentioned.”

Lord Ashworth’s beard practically vibrated. He approached, voice warm and booming. “Tobin, we were discussing these pamphlets. Revolutionary. The ink captures the spirit of our waterways. This isn’t only facts. This is art.”

Tobin stared at him, then at the faces, then at the pages where blue bled with an artistry he could never have manufactured. Steam rose from paper cups and mingled with orange and ink. Calm contemplation, in a room that had been meant for sterile history.

“But the accuracy,” he stammered. “The historical detail.”

Rhea landed on his shoulder, grounding him. She did not give him a lecture about standards. She tapped a pamphlet with one claw, where a swirl happened to follow the curve of a mapped lock. The water on the page looked like water. The letters still told the truth. They simply arrived dressed for weather.

Tobin breathed oranges and ink. He looked at Rhea’s quiet certainty, at Bartholomew’s stained fingers, at Lord Ashworth waiting as if the archivist’s word still mattered. Charts and checklists had their place. So, it seemed, did a press with opinions.

“My Lord,” Tobin said, finding a new firmness, “these pamphlets were not printed as intended. I believe their look captures a spirit of the canals that mere technical precision might miss. If you find them suitable.”

Lord Ashworth clapped him on the back, a hearty thump. “Suitable? My dear Tobin, exquisite. Revolutionary. We shall commission a whole series in this style. We’ll call it the Azure Canal Nouveau.”

Tobin stood in the same workshop where the twilight ink had first behaved. He stacked the blue pages as carefully as he had stacked the black ones, and this time he did not hide the swirls. Bartholomew grinned. Rhea preened. Outside, the canal went on being blue without asking anyone’s permission, and the pamphlets, at last, had decided to agree.
characters: Tobin (an otter canal archivist), Rhea (the kestrel friend)
audience: young adults aged 16-18, teen anthology entry
author: StoryGen Community
